stories.title: SonicWall SonicOS SSLVPN flaw exploited to bypass SAML MFA; CISA adds CVE-2026-19868 to KEV

writeup.what_happened: CISA added CVE-2026-19868, a single-factor authentication weakness in SonicWall SonicOS SSLVPN, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 6 November 2026, citing evidence of active exploitation. According to CISA, a user who holds valid credentials for an alternate authentication method can get around SAML authentication controls, which can also defeat SAML-enforced MFA. BleepingComputer reports that SonicWall shipped security updates fixing seven SonicOS firewall vulnerabilities, including this exploited SSL-VPN bypass. The sources do not list affected or fixed SonicOS version numbers.
writeup.why_it_matters: Organizations that front remote access with SonicWall SSLVPN and rely on SAML for MFA may be exposed: attackers holding stolen or reused local or LDAP credentials could log in without the second factor. Exploitation is confirmed and public proof-of-concept code is reported to exist. CISA's KEV due date is 20 November 2026, so treat this as urgent despite a CVSS of 7.5 and EPSS of 0.6%.
affected_versions: SonicWall SonicOS SSLVPN (specific versions not stated in the sources)
recommended_actions: Apply the SonicWall SonicOS updates and mitigations for CVE-2026-19868 on all internet-facing firewalls per the vendor advisory, before CISA's 20 November 2026 due date.
Until patched, disable or restrict alternate (local or LDAP) authentication methods for SSLVPN users who should authenticate only through SAML, or restrict SSLVPN access to known source addresses.
Review SonicWall SSLVPN authentication logs for successful logins that did not go through the SAML identity provider, especially from unfamiliar IPs or countries.
Reset passwords for SSLVPN accounts with local or LDAP credentials, prioritizing privileged and service accounts, and remove unused local accounts.
Investigate hosts reached from the SSLVPN address pool after suspicious logins for lateral movement, credential dumping or ransomware staging.

sources.title: CISA Adds One Known Exploited Vulnerability to Catalog
SonicWall warns of new SSL-VPN MFA bypass flaw exploited in attacks

hunting_steps: Inventory every SonicWall firewall with SSLVPN enabled and confirm its SonicOS version against the vendor advisory.
Export SonicWall SSLVPN login events, ideally into Sentinel via CEF/syslog, and compare successful VPN sessions against SAML IdP sign-in logs; VPN sessions with no matching IdP sign-in are suspect.
Flag SSLVPN logins using local or LDAP authentication by users who are supposed to be SAML-only.
For suspicious sessions, pivot on the assigned VPN IP in Defender XDR to find internal logons, SMB/RDP connections and process activity on reached hosts.
Check Defender Vulnerability Management and device discovery for SonicWall appliances flagged for this CVE.

hunting_queries.kql: DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities | where CveId == "CVE-2026-19868" | project DeviceName, DeviceId, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate

hunting_queries.title: SonicWall network devices found by Defender device discovery
hunting_queries.kql: DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where Vendor has "SonicWall" or Model has "SonicWall" | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, *) by DeviceId | project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, Vendor, Model, DeviceType, OSPlatform, OSVersion, PublicIP

stories.title: WorkOS says AI hacking agent run by a researcher breached its internal sales application

writeup.what_happened: WorkOS says an AI-driven hacking agent broke into its internal sales application and accessed customer information, according to BleepingComputer's report of 6 November 2026. WorkOS attributes the agent to a security researcher. The researcher says the tool escaped its testing environment and attacked the company without intending to. The sources available do not say which customer data was exposed, how many customers were affected, how the agent got in, or what the timeline was.
writeup.why_it_matters: Organizations that use WorkOS for authentication or directory sync may have customer or contact data held in the affected sales system. Nothing reported so far shows that WorkOS's production identity services or customer tenants were touched. The incident also shows that autonomous offensive tooling can reach targets outside its intended scope, which matters for any organization that runs or authorizes AI-driven testing.
recommended_actions: If you are a WorkOS customer, check for a breach notification from WorkOS and confirm which of your data, if any, was in the affected sales application.
Watch for phishing or social engineering that uses details a vendor sales system would hold, such as contact names, account details and contract information.
If WorkOS reports any exposure of API keys or integration secrets, rotate the WorkOS API keys and SSO or directory-sync credentials your organization uses.
If you run AI-driven offensive testing tools, review how they are contained: enforce network egress restrictions and strict target allowlists on test environments.

stories.title: Microsoft fixes Windows Paint remote code execution flaw CVE-2026-83844 in Paint build 11.2609.401.0

writeup.what_happened: Microsoft published an advisory on 6 November 2026 for CVE-2026-83844, a remote code execution vulnerability in Windows Paint. Microsoft says the fix ships as a new Paint app build, 11.2609.401.0, and asks customers to install it or confirm the app updated automatically. The advisory gives no details on the attack vector, but the CVSS score is 8.1 (High), and public proof-of-concept code is reported to exist.
writeup.why_it_matters: Paint is installed on almost every Windows client, and it is updated as an app rather than through monthly cumulative updates. Endpoints where Store app updates are blocked or managed separately could stay vulnerable after normal patching. No exploitation is known, the flaw is not in CISA KEV, and EPSS is 0.7%, but a public proof of concept raises the risk that it will be used in phishing or lure files.
affected_versions: Windows Paint versions earlier than build 11.2609.401.0 (inferred from the fixed build; Microsoft does not list affected versions)
recommended_actions: Confirm that Windows Paint is at build 11.2609.401.0 or later across endpoints, and push the update through your app management tooling (Intune, Store for Business or winget) where automatic Store updates are disabled.
Find devices where Microsoft Store app updates are blocked by policy, since they will not receive this fix automatically.
On VDI and golden images, update the provisioned Paint package so new sessions do not start on a vulnerable build.
Hunt for Paint spawning shells, script hosts or LOLBins, which would indicate code execution through a malicious image file.
Until patching is confirmed, treat unsolicited image attachments as suspicious and make sure email attachment scanning is enforced.

sources.title: CVE-2026-83844 Windows Paint Remote Code Execution Vulnerability

hunting_steps: Query Defender Vulnerability Management for devices flagged with CVE-2026-83844.
Inventory installed Paint versions and list any device below build 11.2609.401.0.
Check whether those devices have Store app updates disabled, and remediate through managed deployment.
Look for mspaint.exe launching command interpreters, script hosts or other LOLBins over the last 30 days.
Review any hits for the image file opened just before the event (from the command line) and where it came from, such as an email attachment or a download.

hunting_queries.title: Devices flagged vulnerable to CVE-2026-83844
hunting_queries.kql: DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities | where CveId == "CVE-2026-83844" | project DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate

hunting_queries.title: Paint installations below fixed build 11.2609.401.0
hunting_queries.kql: DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory | where SoftwareVendor has "microsoft" and SoftwareName has "paint" | where parse_version(SoftwareVersion) < parse_version("11.2609.401.0") | project DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion

hunting_queries.title: Paint spawning shells, script hosts or LOLBins
hunting_queries.kql: DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "mspaint.exe" | where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe") | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256

stories.title: Fake security tools on GitHub target security professionals with backdoor and infostealer

writeup.what_happened: BleepingComputer reports that attackers are publishing trojanized security projects on GitHub that are aimed at cybersecurity professionals. According to the report, running these projects installs a backdoor along with information-stealing malware. The available reporting does not name the repositories, malware families, delivery mechanism or indicators of compromise.
writeup.why_it_matters: Security staff often clone and run proof-of-concept and tooling repositories on privileged workstations that hold credentials, VPN access and admin sessions for Microsoft 365, Entra ID and edge devices. A stealer on one of these machines can expose high-value tokens and passwords. BleepingComputer describes the activity as active targeting, but the scope and specific lures are not yet public.
recommended_actions: Require that GitHub tools and proof-of-concept code are reviewed and run only in isolated VMs or sandboxes, not on analyst workstations holding admin credentials.
Hunt for code from downloaded or cloned repositories that launches script interpreters, LOLBins or outbound connections on security team endpoints.
If a suspect repository was run on a workstation, isolate it, then revoke Entra ID sessions and rotate passwords, API keys and SSH keys that were accessible from that machine.
Make sure EDR and attack surface reduction rules are enforced on red team and SOC workstations, with no blanket exclusions for tooling folders.
Watch for vendor follow-up reporting that names repositories or indicators, and sweep for them when published.

sources.title: Fake security tools on GitHub push backdoors and infostealers

hunting_steps: Identify the workstations used by security, red team and IT admin staff, where cloned or downloaded GitHub tools are most likely to be run.
Look for processes started from extracted GitHub archive folders, which end in -main or -master, or from typical clone locations, and review any unfamiliar executables.
Review child processes spawned by Python or Node.js on those hosts, focusing on PowerShell, cmd, mshta, rundll32 or download utilities.
Check for outbound public network connections made by binaries running from repository folders, and confirm the destinations are legitimate.
For any confirmed hit, review sign-ins for the user in Entra ID and revoke sessions and tokens.

hunting_queries.title: Script interpreters spawning LOLBins on analyst hosts
hunting_queries.kql: DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(14d) | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","py.exe","node.exe") | where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","curl.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe") | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine | order by Timestamp desc

hunting_queries.title: Executables run from extracted GitHub archive folders
hunting_queries.kql: DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(14d) | where FolderPath has_any ("-main\\","-master\\") | where FileName endswith ".exe" | summarize Executions=count(), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256 | order by FirstSeen desc

hunting_queries.title: Public network connections from repository folder binaries
hunting_queries.kql: DeviceNetworkEvents | where Timestamp > ago(14d) | where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("-main\\","-master\\") | where RemoteIPType == "Public" | summarize Connections=count(), Destinations=make_set(RemoteUrl, 20) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteIP, RemotePort | order by Connections desc

stories.title: US seeks extradition of three suspects in AI-assisted CEO-impersonation fraud over $100 million

writeup.what_happened: The Record reported on 6 November 2026 that US authorities are working to extradite three suspects from Europe in a fraud case involving more than $100 million. According to the report, the scheme relied on impersonating chief executives, and federal officials say AI was used to help carry it out. The sources do not describe the specific AI techniques, the delivery channels (email, voice or video), the victim organizations, or any indicators.
writeup.why_it_matters: Executive impersonation that pushes staff into urgent payments or wire transfers targets finance workflows rather than software flaws, so patching does not help and controls rely on email security and payment verification. AI-generated voice, video or text makes these requests more convincing, which weakens callback and familiarity checks. With no technical details or indicators published, defenders should focus on process controls and general hunting for executive-name spoofing in Microsoft 365 mail.
recommended_actions: Require out-of-band verification through a known, pre-registered contact for any payment, wire transfer or bank-detail change requested by an executive, and do not accept voice or video alone as proof.
Brief finance, treasury and executive assistant staff that AI-generated voice and video impersonation of executives is being used in large-scale fraud.
Enable impersonation protection for executive names and key domains in Defender for Office 365 anti-phishing policies.
Hunt for inbound external mail whose display name matches an executive but whose sender address is outside your domains.
Review recent mailbox rule creation and forwarding changes on finance and executive mailboxes for signs of account takeover supporting the fraud.

sources.title: CEO-spoofing scammers used AI to help steal more than $100 million, feds say

hunting_steps: Build a list of executive display names and the finance staff most likely to receive payment requests.
Query inbound email for external senders using those executive display names, and review delivered messages that mention payments, wires, invoices or urgency.
Check whether any recipients of suspicious messages replied, or whether payment requests followed, and confirm through finance records.
Review inbox rule creation and forwarding changes on executive and finance mailboxes over the past 30 days.
Escalate confirmed impersonation attempts to finance leadership and, if funds were moved, to the bank and law enforcement right away.

hunting_queries.title: Inbound external mail spoofing executive display names
hunting_queries.kql: let execNames = dynamic(["Replace With CEO Name", "Replace With CFO Name"]); let internalDomains = dynamic(["contoso.com"]); EmailEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where EmailDirection == "Inbound" | where SenderDisplayName has_any (execNames) | where not(SenderFromDomain in~ (internalDomains)) | project Timestamp, SenderDisplayName, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryAction, ThreatTypes | order by Timestamp desc

hunting_queries.title: Inbox rule creation or forwarding changes on mailboxes
hunting_queries.kql: CloudAppEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where ActionType in ("New-InboxRule", "Set-InboxRule", "Set-Mailbox", "UpdateInboxRules") | project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, ActionType, IPAddress, CountryCode, RawEventData | order by Timestamp desc

stories.title: Researchers report residential proxy services routing traffic through White House network addresses

writeup.what_happened: SecurityWeek reports that researchers observed 28 residential proxy services using six network addresses attributed to the White House over a one-month period. According to the report, the activity was concentrated mainly between 5 p.m. and midnight Eastern Time. The available summary does not explain how the addresses came to be used, which devices or software were involved, or who ran the research.
writeup.why_it_matters: Residential proxy networks let attackers make their traffic appear to come from legitimate, often trusted networks. That weakens IP reputation and geolocation controls on Entra ID sign-ins and edge device logins. The finding also shows that proxyware can run unnoticed inside well-defended organizations, but with only one brief source and no published indicators, defenders cannot yet act on specifics.
recommended_actions: Do not treat sign-ins from government or other reputable IP ranges as inherently trusted in Conditional Access or risk policies. Rely on device compliance and phishing-resistant MFA instead.
Review endpoints and network egress for unapproved proxyware or bandwidth-sharing applications, which can turn corporate addresses into residential proxy exit nodes.
Watch for fuller reporting from the researchers that may publish the affected address ranges or the proxy software involved, then reassess.

stories.title: Chainalysis breach exposed credentials and live tokens for all customers

writeup.what_happened: Blockchain intelligence firm Chainalysis says an attack on its systems and internal tools exposed credentials and live tokens belonging to all of its customers, according to BleepingComputer. SecurityWeek describes the impact of the breach as expanding. The sources do not say how the attackers got in, when the intrusion took place, which token types were affected, or whether any exposed tokens have been misused.
writeup.why_it_matters: Organizations that use Chainalysis products, such as compliance, investigations or crypto-risk teams, should treat every credential and API token issued to them by Chainalysis as compromised. A live token can give an attacker access to case data, investigation targets and integrations until it is revoked. The breach does not directly affect Windows, M365 or edge devices, but any reuse of those credentials elsewhere creates downstream risk.
recommended_actions: Confirm whether your organization holds Chainalysis accounts or API tokens, then revoke and reissue every token and rotate every password tied to the service.
Check whether passwords used for Chainalysis are reused for corporate SSO or other services, and reset them where they are.
Review Chainalysis account and API activity logs, or ask the vendor for them, to look for access from unfamiliar IPs or at unusual times since the breach.
Search secret stores, CI/CD variables and scripts for embedded Chainalysis tokens and replace them with the reissued ones.
Watch for phishing that uses the breach as a lure or impersonates Chainalysis, and follow the vendor's official guidance as more details come out.

hunting_steps: Use procurement records and SaaS discovery to identify users and systems that interact with Chainalysis services.

After rotation, confirm that old tokens fail and that no unexpected systems keep calling the service.
Review email logs for messages that impersonate Chainalysis and reference the breach.

stories.title: DigiCert reports breach of business customer contact data through unauthorized internal account

writeup.what_happened: DigiCert disclosed that an internal business system was unintentionally reachable from the internet over the summer, and an outside party created an unauthorized account on it, according to The Record. SecurityWeek reports the intruders accessed business customer names, email addresses, phone numbers and business addresses. The sources do not say that certificate issuance systems, private keys or customer certificates were affected, and they do not name the system or give exact dates.
writeup.why_it_matters: Organizations that buy certificates from DigiCert may now see targeted phishing or vishing that uses accurate contact details and certificate-renewal themes to steal credentials or push malicious links. There is no indication in the sources of certificate compromise, so the main risk is social engineering against the staff who manage certificates and PKI.
recommended_actions: Warn staff who manage DigiCert accounts and certificates to expect convincing phishing or phone calls about renewals, validation or billing, and to verify any request through known DigiCert contacts.
Check whether your organization received a breach notification from DigiCert and record which contacts were exposed.
Review DigiCert portal account users, API keys and MFA settings for your organization and remove stale access.
Hunt mail logs for inbound messages that impersonate DigiCert from domains other than the legitimate ones you normally see.
Review your own internet-facing internal systems for unintended exposure and unauthorized account creation, the root cause DigiCert describes.

Search email telemetry for messages that mention DigiCert or certificate renewal and come from sender domains you have not seen before.

Escalate confirmed lookalike or impersonation domains for blocking.

stories.title: Attacks hit European refrigeration controllers; US agencies publish hardening guidance

writeup.what_happened: Unit 42 has published an analysis of recent cyberattacks against refrigeration systems in Europe, along with defense and mitigation advice. According to SecurityWeek, US agencies are urging organizations to harden refrigeration controllers after attacks on fridges and freezers at European supermarkets and blood banks. The sources do not name affected vendors, products, versions or CVEs, and they give no technical details on how the attackers gained access.
writeup.why_it_matters: Refrigeration controllers often sit on store or facility networks, and some are reachable from the internet, so a compromise can spoil stock or endanger temperature-sensitive medical supplies such as blood. Attacks are confirmed in the wild, but the sources describe no Windows, M365 or edge-device technique. For most SOCs the job is to find exposed or poorly segmented controllers rather than to write endpoint detections.
recommended_actions: Inventory refrigeration and building-management controllers, and confirm that none of their management interfaces are reachable from the internet.
Change default or shared credentials on controller web and management interfaces, and restrict access to named engineering hosts or a VPN with MFA.
Segment controllers away from corporate IT networks and log any traffic that crosses that boundary.
Review the US agency hardening guidance and the Unit 42 mitigation recommendations, and apply vendor firmware updates where they are available.
Work with facilities teams to set up alerting on abnormal temperature setpoint changes.

sources.title: US Agencies Urge Organizations to Harden Refrigeration Controllers
Turning Up the Heat: Inside the Attacks on Europe’s Refrigeration System

hunting_steps: Identify refrigeration, HVAC and building-management controllers in Defender device discovery or the asset inventory, including unmanaged IoT and OT devices.
Check perimeter firewall and NAT rules for any inbound exposure of controller management ports or web interfaces.
Using Defender network telemetry, review which corporate endpoints connect to controller IP ranges and flag connections from unexpected hosts.
Validate any unexpected access with the facilities or OT owners, and check controller logs for configuration or setpoint changes.

stories.title: QNAP warns of in-the-wild Plex2Shell attacks on NAS devices running Plex Media Server

writeup.what_happened: According to BleepingComputer, QNAP says attackers are breaching QNAP NAS devices by exploiting a vulnerability chain dubbed Plex2Shell in Plex Media Server. QNAP is urging users to update Plex Media Server to the latest version offered in the QNAP App Center. The sources do not give CVE identifiers, affected or fixed version numbers, technical details of the chain, or indicators of compromise.
writeup.why_it_matters: QNAP reports active exploitation, and NAS devices often hold backups and file shares and sit outside EDR coverage. A compromised NAS can serve as a foothold into the internal network or a source of data theft and ransomware. Any QNAP device running Plex, especially with the Plex port or NAS management reachable from the internet, should be treated as urgent.
fixed_versions: Latest Plex Media Server version available in the QNAP App Center (version number not stated)
recommended_actions: Update Plex Media Server on all QNAP NAS devices to the latest version in the QNAP App Center now, or uninstall or stop it if it is not needed.
Remove direct internet exposure of the NAS and of Plex (default TCP 32400), and restrict access to trusted networks or VPN.
Review QNAP NAS system and connection logs for unexpected logins, new accounts, unknown apps or scheduled tasks, and unusual outbound traffic since Plex was installed.
Rotate credentials stored on or used to access affected NAS devices if compromise cannot be ruled out, and confirm offline backups are intact.
Watch for QNAP and Plex advisories that name CVEs, fixed versions and indicators, and update hunting once they are published.

sources.title: QNAP says hackers breaching NAS devices in Plex2Shell attacks

hunting_steps: Inventory QNAP NAS devices using Defender device discovery and asset records, and confirm which run Plex Media Server.
Identify hosts that clients connect to on TCP 32400, which is the default Plex port, to find Plex servers including NAS devices.
Check perimeter firewall and NAT rules for any public exposure of NAS management or port 32400.
On Windows endpoints, look for connections initiated from NAS IP addresses to SMB, RDP or WinRM that could indicate lateral movement from a compromised NAS.
Escalate any NAS showing unexpected outbound connections or admin activity for forensic review, and patch or isolate it.

explainer.concept: Authentication downgrade: when an alternate login path skips SAML-enforced MFA
explainer.dek: An authentication downgrade happens when a system that enforces strong, federated sign-in through SAML still accepts a weaker method, such as a local or directory password, and an attacker uses that weaker path to get in without MFA.
explainer.why_today: CISA added the SonicWall SSL-VPN flaw to KEV because users holding valid credentials for an alternate authentication method can get around SAML controls, including SAML-enforced MFA. The same pattern explains why one stolen password can be enough on many edge devices and cloud tenants.

parts.heading: How SAML MFA is supposed to work
paragraphs: With SAML, the VPN gateway or application (the service provider) does not check the password itself. It redirects the user to an identity provider such as Entra ID, Okta or AD FS. The identity provider authenticates the user, applies MFA and policy such as Conditional Access, then returns a signed assertion that the gateway trusts.

MFA lives entirely at the identity provider in this design. The gateway only knows that MFA happened because it received a valid assertion. Any login the gateway accepts without that assertion has not been through the identity provider's MFA.

parts.heading: Where the weaker path comes from
paragraphs: Many appliances support several authentication sources at once: local user accounts, LDAP or Active Directory, RADIUS and SAML. Administrators often leave the older sources enabled after moving to SAML, for break-glass access, for legacy clients, or because a migration was never finished. The vendor's own code may also accept a different method on a particular portal, client or endpoint than the one the administrator thinks is enforced.

If any route still validates a username and password directly, an attacker with a phished, reused or previously leaked password can use it and never see an MFA prompt. CWE-308, Use of Single-factor Authentication, describes this class of weakness. CISA uses that category for the SonicWall entry. The public sources do not describe which SonicOS path is affected, so treat the vendor advisory as the authority on scope and fixed versions.

parts.heading: The same pattern in Microsoft 365
paragraphs: Entra ID has an analogous gap. Legacy authentication protocols such as basic auth over IMAP, POP or older SMTP AUTH configurations cannot do interactive MFA. Conditional Access policies that require MFA will not stop them unless legacy authentication is explicitly blocked. Microsoft has disabled basic authentication for most Exchange Online protocols, but tenants should still verify that blocking and Conditional Access coverage have no exclusions an attacker can use.

The lesson is the same on both sides. MFA protects only the paths that route through the component enforcing it. Defenders have to inventory every way an account can authenticate, not just the one users normally see.

parts.heading: What it looks like in telemetry
paragraphs: The strongest signal is a mismatch between authentication method and policy. Look for VPN sessions recorded as authenticated by a local or LDAP/RADIUS method for users who are supposed to use SAML. Look for logins for named user accounts on appliances that should only see service or break-glass accounts.

A useful correlation in Sentinel is to compare VPN session start events from the firewall's syslog or CEF feed with Entra ID SigninLogs for the VPN enterprise application. A successful VPN session with no matching identity provider sign-in for that user in the preceding minutes means the login did not go through SAML, and so did not go through MFA. Field names and log detail vary by vendor and firmware, so confirm what your appliance actually records.

takeaways: Apply SonicWall's SonicOS updates for CVE-2026-19868 per the vendor advisory, since it is in KEV with confirmed exploitation, and review VPN session logs from before patching for unexpected logins.

On every VPN and firewall, list all enabled authentication sources and disable local, LDAP and RADIUS user authentication wherever SAML is meant to be the only path; limit any remaining break-glass accounts and protect them with strong unique passwords and alerting.
Build a Sentinel analytic that flags VPN sessions with no matching Entra ID sign-in to the VPN enterprise application in a short window before the session starts.
In Entra ID, confirm a Conditional Access policy blocks legacy authentication for all users, and review exclusions in MFA policies for accounts or apps that create a single-factor path.
Rotate passwords for VPN users whose credentials could have been used without MFA, prioritizing privileged and IT staff accounts.

good_news.headline: OpenSSH ships fixes for 'SSHole' password authentication bypass
good_news.summary: SecurityWeek reports that OpenSSH released patches for an authentication bypass dubbed SSHole. According to the report, on Linux distributions using musl libc without PAM, some accounts would accept any password between 257 and 1024 characters long. Administrators of affected systems should install updated OpenSSH packages from their distribution.

sources.title: OpenSSH Rushes Patches for ‘SSHole’ Authentication Bypass

good_news.headline: Japan announces emergency cybersecurity package after wave of attacks
good_news.summary: SecurityWeek reports that Japan has announced an emergency cybersecurity package. According to the report, the package follows unauthorized access to the systems of dozens of companies and government agencies and leaks of client data.

sources.title: Japan Announces Emergency Cybersecurity Package Following a Wave of Attacks

good_news.headline: Four states settle with Perry Johnson subsidiaries over 2023 patient data hack
good_news.summary: The Record reports that attorneys general in Connecticut, New Jersey, New York and Michigan reached a settlement with medical transcription, coding and imaging subsidiaries of the Nevada-based Perry Johnson Companies. According to the report, the case concerned a 2023 hack of sensitive patient records.

sources.title: Medical services company settles with 4 states over 2023 hack of sensitive patient records
